title: Fractions
goal: Compare, simplify, add and multiply fractions, and know why a denominator cannot be 0.
generalHint: Put both fractions on the same strip. Check the denominators first.

next.title: Square root of 2 is not a fraction

screens.label: RECALL
screens.title: Does 4 divide 15?

options.label: Yes
options.reply: Write 15 as 4 × an integer. 4 · 3 = 12 and 4 · 4 = 16. Is there an integer k with 15 = 4k?

hints: Look for an integer k with 15 = 4k.

screens.label: PUZZLE
screens.title: Two quarters or one half?
screens.prompt: A bar is cut into 4 equal pieces. You take 2 pieces. Is this more than 1/2 of the same bar? Guess before you look.

options.label: More
options.reply: The bar has more pieces, but the pieces are smaller. Compare the shaded length, not the number of pieces.

options.label: Less
options.reply: 2 pieces out of 4 is a lot of the bar. Compare it with 1 piece out of 2.

feedback.correctTitle: Good guess. It is the same length.
feedback.correctWhy: 2 pieces out of 4 make the same length as 1 piece out of 2.

screens.caption: Pick one, then check.

screens.label: EXPLORE
screens.title: Cut the strip finer
screens.prompt: Cut each piece of the strip in two. The shaded length stays the same. After 2 cuts, find the number of shaded pieces.

answer.correctWhy: After 2 cuts the strip has 8 pieces. 4 of them make the same shaded length as 1 of 2.

mistakes.reply: That is the number before the cuts. Each cut doubles the number of shaded pieces too. How many now?
That is the number after 1 cut. After 2 cuts, you have 8 pieces. How many are shaded?

hints: Each cut doubles the pieces and the shaded pieces.
screens.caption: Cut the strip 2 times, then check.

screens.label: NAME IT
screens.title: Rational numbers
screens.prompt: A rational number is a quotient $m/n$, with integers $m$ and $n$ and $n \ne 0$. A strip cut into 0 pieces has no pieces. A finite decimal is rational: $1.4 = 14/10$. Each integer $m$ is $m/1$.

interaction.question: Which one is not a rational number?

options.reply: 3/1 = 3. Each integer m is m/1. Which fraction has 0 below the line?
0/5 = 0. The top may be 0. Which fraction has 0 below the line?

feedback.correctWhy: The denominator cannot be 0. A strip cut into 0 pieces has no pieces.

screens.label: NAME IT
screens.title: Cross−multiplication
screens.prompt: Two fractions are equal when their cross products are equal. Lang assumes this rule here. Lesson 1.8 proves it.

screens.label: NAME IT
screens.title: Cancel and move a minus
screens.prompt: You can cancel a common factor $a \ne 0$. A minus sign can move from the top to the bottom. Lang proves both with cross−multiplication.

screens.label: PROVE IT
screens.title: The lowest form
screens.prompt: Prove Theorem 3: each positive rational number has a lowest form. Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of $m$ and $n$.

lines.math: \text{Let } d \text{ be the greatest common divisor of } m \text{ and } n
\text{So } de > d \text{ divides } m \text{ and } n
\text{This is impossible, so } e \text{ does not exist}

steps.label: a divisor goes into both numbers
de is a bigger common divisor
d was the greatest, so this is impossible

wrongReasonReplies.cancel-frac: The cancellation rule removes a common factor from the top and the bottom. Is there a common factor in the line before?
wrongReasonReplies.cross-mul: The cross−multiplication rule tests if two fractions are equal. Does this line compare two fractions?
wrongReasonReplies.thm-2-cor: This rule is about even numbers and squares. Is there a square here?
wrongReasonReplies.div: This step says that a divisor goes into both numbers, so each number is that divisor times an integer. Is a divisor named in the line before?
wrongReasonReplies.put-in: This step puts the values from the line before into the expression. Did you use m = dr and n = ds here?
wrongReasonReplies.suppose: This step starts the argument by contradiction: suppose there is a common divisor e > 1. Is this the start of the argument?
wrongReasonReplies.bigger: This step compares de with d. Does the line say that de is a common divisor of m and n?
wrongReasonReplies.greatest: This step uses that d was the greatest common divisor. Is there a contradiction in the line before?

feedback.correctWhy: The only common divisor of r and s is 1. So m/n = r/s is in lowest form.

screens.caption: Tap a reason to fill the orange slot.

screens.label: EXPLORE
screens.title: Add on one strip
screens.prompt: Add $3/5 + 8/5$ on one strip. The pieces have the same size, so you add the numbers of pieces.

answer.correctWhy: 3 pieces and 8 pieces of size 1/5 make 11 pieces of size 1/5.

mistakes.reply: That adds the tops and the bottoms: 11/10. The pieces keep the size 1/5. How many pieces in all?

hints: Add the shaded pieces. The size of the pieces stays 1/5.
screens.caption: Tap the strip to add, then check.

screens.label: EXPLORE
screens.title: Add with a common denominator
screens.prompt: Now add $2/3 + 1/4$. The pieces have different sizes. Cut both strips into 12 pieces first.

answer.correctWhy: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12. The pieces have the same size, so you add the numbers of pieces.

mistakes.reply: You added the tops and the bottoms. Put both fractions on the strip. Is 3/7 longer than 2/3?

screens.caption: Tap the strips, then check.

screens.label: NAME IT
screens.title: Adding fractions
screens.prompt: To add fractions with different denominators, put them over a common denominator. The rules for adding integers stay true for rational numbers.

note.label: LANG ASSUMES
note.text: The rules of addition and multiplication stay true for rational numbers. So the proofs from lesson 1.2 stay true.

screens.label: NAME IT
screens.title: Multiplying fractions
screens.prompt: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. Cancel before you multiply. For powers, $(m/n)^k = m^k / n^k$.

options.reply: You cubed only the 2. The rule is (m/n)ᵏ = mᵏ/nᵏ. What is 3³?
You multiplied 2 and 3 by 3. A power means repeated multiplication. What is 2 · 2 · 2?

hints: Cube the top and cube the bottom.

screens.label: EXPLORE
screens.title: A substance that halves
screens.prompt: 40 g of a substance halves every 6 minutes. Tap to halve it 3 times, for 18 minutes. Find the mass.

answer.correctWhy: 40 g halves 3 times: 20, 10, 5. This is 40/2³ = 5 g.

mistakes.reply: That is the mass after 2 halvings. 18 minutes are 3 periods of 6 minutes. Halve once more.
That divides 40 by 3. The mass halves 3 times, so divide by 2³.

screens.caption: Halve 3 times, then check.

screens.label: PRACTICE · 1 OF 4
screens.title: Are they equal?

options.label: No, $48 \ne 108$
options.reply: Multiply across the diagonals: top−left by bottom−right, then bottom−left by top−right.

feedback.correctWhy: 6 · 12 = 72 and 9 · 8 = 72. The cross products are equal.

hints: Multiply 6 · 12 and 9 · 8. Compare the two products.

steps.text: Multiply the top of the first fraction by the bottom of the second.
Multiply the top of the second fraction by the bottom of the first. 72 = 72.

options.label: No, $24 \ne 150$
options.reply: Multiply across the diagonals: top−left by bottom−right, then bottom−left by top−right.

feedback.correctWhy: 4 · 15 = 60 and 10 · 6 = 60. The cross products are equal.

screens.label: PRACTICE · 2 OF 4
screens.title: Lowest form

options.reply: 9 and 12 are both divisible by 3. Divide both again.
6 and 8 are both divisible by 2. Divide both again.

feedback.correctWhy: The greatest common divisor of 18 and 24 is 6. 18/24 = 3/4.

hints: Find the greatest number that divides both 18 and 24.

options.reply: 10 and 15 are both divisible by 5. Divide both again.
4 and 6 are both divisible by 2. Divide both again.

feedback.correctWhy: The greatest common divisor of 20 and 30 is 10. 20/30 = 2/3.

screens.label: PRACTICE · 3 OF 4
screens.title: Add fractions
screens.prompt: Find the sum. You can type a fraction, for example 5/6.

mistakes.reply: You added the tops and the bottoms. Put both fractions on the strip. Is 3/7 longer than 2/3?
That is only 1/4 on the 12−piece strip. Add the 8/12 for 2/3 too.

screens.label: PRACTICE · 4 OF 4
screens.title: Multiply and cancel

answer.correctWhy: Cancel 4 and 8 to 1 and 2, and 3 and 9 to 1 and 3. Then 1 · 2 over 1 · 3 = 2/3.

mistakes.reply: You added the tops and the bottoms. To multiply, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. What is 3 · 8?

hints: 4 divides 8. 3 divides 9. Cancel before you multiply.

steps.text: Multiply the tops and the bottoms.

screens.label: LESSON 1.6 COMPLETE
screens.title: Fractions, rules and proofs.

options.label: True
options.reply: You added the tops and the bottoms. Put both fractions on a strip. Is 2/5 longer than 1/2?

screens.caption: Saved to your rule book.
